notes: First-refresh audit, 2026-09-01. THE SWEEP FINDING WAS HALF RIGHT AND ITS PROPOSED FIX WAS ALSO WRONG: the article said the Nazis looted "an estimated one million artworks"; the sweep proposed "as many as 650,000" from data/ref-text/bill-114-s-2763.txt. That figure is from S. 2763 (114th) AS INTRODUCED, a bill that never became law - H.R. 6130 was the vehicle - and the ENACTED text (P.L. 114-308, Sec. 2(1)) reads "hundreds of thousands of works of art and other property". The enacted wording is what the article now carries. Also fixed: the voice-vote/unanimous-consent conflation (Senate by UC 2025-12-10, House by voice vote under suspension 2026-03-16); laches presented as a synonym for an expired statute of limitations; the 2016 enactment date, six-year discovery period and December 31, 2026 deadline, previously supported only by the introduced Senate companion, now sourced to the enacted law. Removed outright (no source): "a problem that had frustrated victims families for decades"; "even when the original claim was valid"; "Passage by unanimous consent ... reflects how uncontroversial it was"; "did not generate organized opposition"; and the unnamed "legal scholars" paragraph. Added (previously omitted changes the law actually makes): new Section 5(g) nationwide service of process, new Section 6 severability, and - added on the sign-off round - the SEC. 2(a)(1)(C) rewrite of the 2016 finding on alternative dispute resolution (striking "will yield just and fair resolutions in a more efficient and predictable manner", inserting "may, in some circumstances, yield just and fair resolutions as well") together with the SEC. 2(a)(2) purposes insert. Also clarified on that round: the replacement filing-window phrase is inserted INTO the 2016 Act, so its "this Act" is the 2016 Act (approved December 16, 2016), while the 2025 Act own applicability provision uses the same words for April 13, 2026; and the rule of construction is redesignated (f) to (i) rather than merely "left in place". FROZEN-TEXT SONNET ROUND returned 0 BLOCKING, 5 advisory; two were applied - a comma the article had added INSIDE a quotation before the Von Saher parenthetical (the enrolled text has none there), and a fifth omitted amendment, the SEC. 2(a)(3)(F)(i) strike of "Subsection (a)" for "Subsections (a), (b), (f), and (g)", which is what carries the 2016 Act own timing rule onto the new (b), (f) and (g). Declined with reason: the title word "voted" (both chambers did vote, by UC and by voice, and the body states plainly that neither produced a recorded vote); the meta description naming only the filing deadline and not also the January 1, 2027 sunset (a simplification the body corrects in full, and the description is already at length); and the bullet heading "Overrides the foreign-sovereign-immunity barrier" (a label on operative text that itself opens "Notwithstanding any other law or prior judicial decision"). CONVERGENCE ROUND (round 5, frozen text, fresh Sonnet) returned 0 BLOCKING, 2 advisory, NEITHER applied and both recorded here so a later round does not re-raise them: (i) the SEC. 2(a)(3)(B) redesignation of subsection (e) to (h) and the SEC. 2(a)(3)(E) conforming cross-reference are label-only amendments with no effect on any partys rights - the "What S. 1884 Actually Changed" list is deliberately a list of SUBSTANTIVE changes, and the (f)-to-(i) move is mentioned only because a sentence about the rule of construction needed it; (ii) the "What It Means for Pending Cases" reasoning is the articles own inference chained from verbatim-quoted conditions, which is explanation of sourced text rather than an unsourced factual assertion. Two consecutive rounds now return 0 blocking on unchanged prose.

claims.claim: The law bars laches and other passage-of-time defenses

claims.sourceSpan: Approved April 13, 2026.

claims.claim: The stated purpose of the Act is to clarify the 2016 Act and appropriately limit passage-of-time and other non-merits defenses
claims.sourceSpan: To clarify the Holocaust Expropriated Art Recovery Act of 2016, to appropriately limit the application of defenses based on the passage of time and other non-merits defenses to claims under that Act.

claims.claim: Congress found in the 2016 Act that it is estimated the Nazis confiscated or misappropriated hundreds of thousands of works of art and other property throughout Europe
claims.sourceSpan: It is estimated that the Nazis confiscated or otherwise misappropriated hundreds of thousands of works of art and other property throughout Europe as part of their genocidal campaign against the Jewish people and other persecuted groups.

claims.claim: The Act says this has been described as the greatest displacement of art in human history
claims.sourceSpan: This has been described as the ``greatest displacement of art in human history''

claims.claim: The Act defines its covered period as beginning January 1, 1933 and ending December 31, 1945
claims.sourceSpan: The term ``covered period'' means the period beginning on January 1, 1933, and ending on December 31, 1945.

claims.claim: The 2016 findings record that recovery lawsuits face significant procedural obstacles partly due to State statutes of limitations
claims.sourceSpan: These lawsuits face significant procedural obstacles partly due to State statutes of limitations, which typically bar claims within some limited number of years from either the date of the loss or the date that the claim should have been discovered.

claims.claim: The 2016 findings record that in some cases the claims expired before World War II even ended
claims.sourceSpan: In some cases, this means that the claims expired before World War II even ended.

claims.claim: The 2016 Act set a six-year clock running from actual discovery rather than from the loss

claims.claim: Discovery is also measured from a possessory interest of the claimant in the artwork
claims.sourceSpan: a possessory interest of the claimant in the artwork or other property

claims.claim: The 2025 Act finds that some courts frustrated the 2016 Act by dismissing lawsuits on passage-of-time defenses such as laches
